title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Course Learning objectives

Define epidemiology and key associated terminology, especially confounding.
Distinguish among association, prediction, and causation.
Explain the Rothman model of sufficient-component causes (RMSCC) and the concept of multifactorial causation.
Explain the limitations of anecdotal evidence in drawing epidemiologic conclusions.
Explain why disseminating risk information is sometimes necessary but rarely sufficient to improve population health.

title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
What is Epidemiology?



EPIDEMIOLOGY

epi – “on, upon”
demo – “people”
ology – “study of”

Definition: the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events (e.g. infectious disease) in specified (human) populations and the application of this study to control health problems
-– James Last, 1995, A Dictionary of Epidemiology

title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Scenario Exercise



Scenario: A city health department notices that one neighborhood has twice the rate of asthma ER visits compared to another neighborhood in the same city. This difference has been observed every year for the past three years.
Questions: Do you think this difference is mostly due to random chance—yes or no? If it’s not random, what is one thing that might explain the difference?
What are we assuming if we believe those factors matter?

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#assumptions-of-epidemiology
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#assumptions-of-epidemiology
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Assumptions of Epidemiology



ASSUMPTION 1
Human disease does not occur at random
Disease frequency and distribution vary because of identifiable factors that increase or decrease risk.


ASSUMPTION 2
Determinants of disease can be identified
Causal and preventive factors can be studied through systematic investigation of populations.

text:
Descriptive and Analytic Epidemiology
Descriptive Epidemiology Is A Necessary Antecedent Of Analytic Epidemiology 


DISTRIBUTION
Descriptive epidemiology

When was the population affected?
Where was the population affected?
Who was affected?



DETERMINANTS
Analytic epidemiology

How was the population affected?
Why was the population affected?

href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#cholera-outbreak-in-london
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Cholera Outbreak In London



Cholera Symptoms
Cholera is an extremely virulent disease that can cause severe acute watery diarrhea. Cholera affects both children and adults and can kill within hours if untreated.
It takes between 12 hours and 5 days for a person to show symptoms after ingesting contaminated food or water.

text:
Micro-Activity: Thinking Like an Epidemiologist

Watch the short video on John Snow and cholera. John Snow: Pioneer of Epidemiology
As you watch, focus on these questions:
What patterns did Snow observe? (Who, where, when — descriptive epidemiology)
What explanation was he testing? (How, why — analytic epidemiology)
Descriptive epidemiology comes first, analytic epidemiology builds on it.

title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
History of Epidemiology: Key Events










Event
Time Period
Description




Bubonic Plague Epidemics (Black Death)
1347 - 1351
One of the deadliest pandemics, causing 75–200 million deaths in Eurasia.


Development of Toxicology
16th Century
Paracelsus, “Father of Toxicology,” introduced the principle: “The dose makes the poison.”


Development of Biostatistics
18th Century
John Graunt pioneered statistical analysis, using Bills of Mortality to study disease patterns in London.


Development of Smallpox Vaccine
1796
Edward Jenner created the first vaccine by using cowpox to confer immunity to smallpox.


1918 Influenza Pandemic
1918-19
The “Spanish flu” infected a third of the global population, killing 50–100 million.


Identification of Smoking as a Cause of Cancer
1950
Landmark studies linked smoking to lung cancer, driving public health campaigns against tobacco use.


Eradication of Smallpox
1980
WHO declared smallpox eradicated, marking the success of global vaccination efforts.

From Patterns to Classification



01
Endemic


02
Epidemic


03
Pandemic


We use person, place, and time to describe disease patterns. These patterns are commonly classified as endemic, epidemic, and pandemic. These terms describe patterns over time and place, not disease severity.

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#disease-distribution-patterns
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#disease-distribution-patterns
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Disease Distribution Patterns


01
Endemic
Disease or condition consistently present in a population

Relatively stable over time
Expected level of occurrence in a given place



02
Epidemic (Outbreak)
Disease occurrence in excess of what is normally expected

Sudden increase over a short period
Often limited to a specific region



03
Pandemic
An epidemic that spreads across multiple countries or continents

Global distribution
Affects a large proportion of the population

objectID: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#exercise-check-your-understanding-1
href: Module 01 - Welcome and Overview/Introduction to Epidemiology/Introduction to Epidemiology.html#exercise-check-your-understanding-1
title: Introduction to Epidemiology
text:
Exercise: Check Your Understanding

A pandemic is always a form of epidemic.

Answer: True
Explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents. It still meets the definition of an epidemic—occurrence in excess of what is normally expected—but on a global scale.

An endemic disease always represents an epidemic.

Answer: False
Explanation: An endemic disease is consistently present at an expected level within a population or region. Because it does not exceed normal expectations, it is not considered an epidemic, even though cases may occur continuously.



[Sources]

Yan Zhang, APHS 20203 W1-Overview and Epi Intro.pptx, source slide 36.

[/Sources]
